topics.name: Types and components of computer systems

questions.q: Which is an example of system software?
questions.why: System software runs the computer; application software does user tasks.

questions.q: RAM is best described as
o: volatile memory that holds data in use
questions.why: Its contents are lost when power is off.

questions.q: Which type of memory holds the start-up instructions and is not lost when power is off?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some candidates gave RAM rather than ROM; RAM is volatile.

questions.q: What is a major advantage of a Graphical User Interface (GUI) over a Command Line Interface (CLI)?
o: It uses significantly less RAM and CPU processing power
It executes batch operations faster for advanced administrators
It is intuitive and accessible with icons and pointers without memorising commands
It does not require a visual monitor
questions.why: GUIs use WIMP (windows, icons, menus, pointer) metaphors that allow everyday users to interact visually without typing command syntax.

questions.q: Which technology overlays computer-generated images onto a live view of the real world, for example through a phone camera?
questions.why: Augmented reality adds digital content on top of the real view; virtual reality replaces the real world with a fully computer-generated one.

long.q: Describe the differences between RAM and ROM, and give one use of each.
scheme: B1: RAM is volatile: its contents are lost when the power is off
B1: RAM holds the programs and data currently in use, and can be read and written
B1: ROM is non-volatile and read-only: contents are kept without power
B1: ROM holds the start-up (boot) instructions

long.q: Compare a Graphical User Interface (GUI) with a Command Line Interface (CLI), and explain why network administrators often prefer a CLI.
scheme: B1: GUI uses visual elements (windows, icons, menus, pointer - WIMP), making it accessible for non-technical users
B1: CLI requires users to type specific syntax commands from memory, demanding higher technical training
B1: CLI requires far less RAM and processor overhead, allowing it to run over low-bandwidth remote connections
B1: CLI supports powerful scripting and batch execution of administrative tasks across hundreds of remote servers

long.q: Explain the difference between system software and application software, giving one example of each.
scheme: B1: system software runs and manages the computer's hardware and provides a platform for other programs
B1: an example of system software, e.g. an operating system, a device driver, a utility such as anti-virus, a compiler
B1: application software lets the user carry out a specific task
B1: an example of application software, e.g. a word processor, spreadsheet, web browser, photo editor

long.q: A sales representative spends most of the week visiting clients. Explain two advantages and one disadvantage of giving them a tablet computer instead of a desktop computer.
scheme: B1: an advantage, e.g. it is light and portable, so it can be carried to every client and used anywhere
B1: a second advantage, e.g. built-in battery, touch screen, camera and mobile/Wi-Fi connection let them show products and send orders on the spot
B1: a disadvantage, e.g. small screen and on-screen keyboard make long typing hard; less processing power and storage; easier to lose or have stolen; limited battery life

long.q: Describe what is meant by artificial intelligence (AI) and give two examples of how AI is used.
scheme: B1: AI is a computer system that simulates human intelligence, e.g. learning from data, reasoning or making decisions
B1: one use, e.g. a voice assistant or chatbot that understands spoken or typed questions
B1: a second use, e.g. self-driving cars, recommending products or films, face recognition, spam filtering

questions.q: Which is a direct data entry device?
questions.why: It captures data without typing.

questions.q: A sensor in a greenhouse is an
questions.why: It sends readings to the computer.

questions.q: Which is an input device?
questions.why: Actuators and speakers are output devices.

questions.q: Which input technology is used to read bank cheques quickly and reliably even if written over?
questions.why: Cheques use magnetic ink with iron oxide; MICR readers sense magnetic fields so signatures or dirt across the line do not hinder reading.

questions.q: A school wants to mark multiple-choice answer sheets automatically, where students shade a box for each answer. Which input method is most suitable?
questions.why: OMR detects the position of shaded marks on a form, which is exactly what an answer sheet needs; OCR reads printed characters and MICR reads magnetic ink.

long.q: A supermarket uses barcode readers at its checkouts. Give two advantages of barcode readers over typing in product codes, and one disadvantage.
scheme: B1: faster data entry, so shorter queues
B1: more accurate: avoids typing errors
B1: a disadvantage, e.g. damaged or dirty barcodes won't scan and must be typed; cost of the equipment

long.q: A school marks multiple-choice answer sheets using optical mark recognition (OMR). Describe how OMR reads the sheets and give two advantages over marking them by hand.
scheme: B1: the sheet is scanned and light is shone onto it; shaded boxes reflect less light than blank areas
B1: the position of each mark is detected and compared with the answer key to work out the score
B1: an advantage, e.g. much faster, so hundreds of sheets are marked quickly
B1: a second advantage, e.g. more accurate/no human marking errors; results can be stored and analysed automatically

long.q: A school office needs to print 500 copies of a black-and-white newsletter. Explain why a laser printer is more suitable than an inkjet printer for this job.
scheme: B1: a laser printer prints pages much faster, so 500 copies are finished quickly
B1: a toner cartridge prints many more pages than an ink cartridge, so the cost per page is lower for large volumes
B1: laser output is sharp and does not smudge, and the large paper tray needs less refilling

long.q: Explain what an actuator is and give two examples of actuators in a computer-controlled washing machine.
scheme: B1: an actuator is an output device that turns a signal from the processor into physical action, e.g. movement
B1: an example, e.g. a motor that turns the drum
B1: a second example, e.g. a pump that drains water; a valve/solenoid that lets water in; the heater; the door lock

long.q: An airport attaches RFID tags to passengers' luggage. Describe how RFID is used to track the bags and give two advantages over using barcodes.
scheme: B1: each tag holds a microchip and an antenna storing a unique ID for the bag
B1: a reader sends out radio waves; the tag responds with its data, which is checked against the flight database to show where the bag is
B1: an advantage, e.g. no line of sight is needed, so tags can be read through the bag or at any angle
B1: a second advantage, e.g. many tags can be read at once; read from a greater distance; tags are harder to damage

questions.q: Which has no moving parts?
questions.why: SSDs use flash memory.

questions.q: Magnetic tape is best for
questions.why: Serial access suits archives.

questions.q: Why is a solid-state drive faster than a hard disk drive?
o: It has no moving parts, so data is accessed electronically
questions.why: SSDs also use less power and are more robust.

questions.q: Why are Solid State Drives (SSDs) preferred over magnetic hard disk drives (HDDs) in laptops?
o: They have infinite read-write rewrite cycles
They cost less per gigabyte than optical discs
They have no moving parts, lower latency, and higher shock resistance
questions.why: SSDs use flash memory with zero mechanical latency, consume less power, and withstand physical drops far better than spinning HDDs.

questions.q: Which type of storage reads data by shining a laser at the surface and detecting pits and lands?
questions.why: Optical media such as DVDs and Blu-ray discs are read by a laser; magnetic storage uses read/write heads and solid-state storage has no moving parts.

long.q: Give three reasons why a laptop is more likely to have a solid-state drive (SSD) than a hard disk drive (HDD).
scheme: B1: no moving parts, so it's less likely to be damaged if dropped
B1: faster access to data, so quicker start-up and loading
B1: lighter, smaller or uses less power, so longer battery life

long.q: A company backs up all its data every night onto magnetic tape. Give two reasons why tape is suitable for this and one disadvantage of using tape.
scheme: B1: very large storage capacity, so a whole night's backup fits on one tape
B1: low cost per gigabyte, and tapes can be stored safely off site
B1: disadvantage: serial access, so finding and restoring one particular file is slow

long.q: Describe how data is read from an optical disc such as a DVD.
scheme: B1: the disc spins while a laser beam is shone onto its surface
B1: the surface has pits and lands that reflect the light differently
B1: a sensor detects the reflected light, and the changes are converted into binary 1s and 0s

long.q: Explain why a Blu-ray disc can store more data than a DVD of the same size.
scheme: B1: Blu-ray uses a blue (violet) laser, which has a shorter wavelength than the red laser of a DVD
B1: so the pits and tracks can be smaller and packed closer together
B1: giving a much larger capacity, e.g. about 25 GB per layer compared with about 4.7 GB for a single-layer DVD

long.q: Explain the difference between serial access and direct access to stored data, and name a storage medium that uses each.
scheme: B1: serial access: data is read in order from the start until the required item is reached
B1: a medium using serial access: magnetic tape
B1: direct access: the device goes straight to the location of the required data
B1: a medium using direct access, e.g. hard disk drive, solid-state drive, DVD, memory card

topics.name: Networks and the effects of using them

questions.q: What does a router do?
o: connects a local network to other networks such as the internet
questions.why: It forwards packets between networks.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of cloud storage?
o: files can be accessed from anywhere with internet
questions.why: Access anywhere; relies on connection and the provider.

questions.q: What does a router do on a home network?
o: Connects the home network to the internet and forwards packets
questions.why: Many routers include a wireless access point.

questions.q: What is the main difference between a Local Area Network (LAN) and a Wide Area Network (WAN)?
o: A LAN always uses satellite links while a WAN uses copper cables
A LAN covers a small geographic site while a WAN spans multiple distant geographic locations
A LAN cannot connect to the internet
A WAN is owned and managed by a single private individual
questions.why: LANs are confined to a single building, campus, or home; WANs (like the internet or multinational corporate nets) connect geographically dispersed sites.

questions.q: Which network device sends data only to the device it is meant for, using that device's MAC address?
questions.why: A switch checks the destination MAC address and forwards data only to that device; a hub broadcasts to every device, and a router uses IP addresses to pass data between networks.

long.q: Describe two advantages and two disadvantages of storing files in the cloud rather than on a computer's own hard drive.
scheme: B1: advantage, e.g. files can be reached from any device with an internet connection
B1: a second advantage, e.g. the provider backs up the data; easy to share and work together
B1: disadvantage, e.g. needs a reliable internet connection
B1: a second disadvantage, e.g. security depends on a third party; ongoing subscription cost

long.q: Explain how a proxy server operates to provide security and caching on an educational institution's network.
scheme: B1: the proxy server acts as an intermediary between local client computers and external internet web servers
B1: clients send web requests to the proxy, which hides the client's internal private IP address from the outside world
B1: proxy server caches frequently visited web pages on local storage, reducing external WAN bandwidth consumption
B1: proxy server checks requested URLs against blacklists and content filters, blocking prohibited material

long.q: Describe the functions of a router in a home network.
scheme: B1: it connects the home local area network to the internet (another network)
B1: it receives data packets and uses their IP addresses to forward them to the correct device or network
B1: e.g. it gives each device its own local IP address; often acts as a wireless access point; can include a firewall

long.q: Explain the difference between the internet and an intranet, and give one reason why a company would set up an intranet.
scheme: B1: the internet is a worldwide, public network of interconnected networks that anyone can use
B1: an intranet is a private network inside one organisation, reached only by its authorised members
B1: a reason, e.g. to share company information and documents securely with staff only; information is more reliable and controlled

long.q: A company plans to replace many face-to-face meetings with video conferencing. Name two items of hardware each participant needs and describe two disadvantages of video conferencing.
scheme: B1: an item of hardware, e.g. a webcam
B1: a second item, e.g. a microphone; speakers or a headset; a large monitor
B1: a disadvantage, e.g. a poor connection causes lag, frozen video or dropped calls
B1: a second disadvantage, e.g. time-zone differences; less personal contact and body language; cost of equipment and training; security of the call

questions.q: Repetitive strain injury can be reduced by
questions.why: A health issue, not a safety one.

questions.q: Which is a health risk from using a computer for a long time?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): safety and health refer to the user, not damage to the equipment.

questions.q: Which is an effect of microprocessor-controlled devices in the home?
o: More leisure time because chores are automated
questions.why: Consider both positive and negative effects.

questions.q: Which health problem is most reduced by using an adjustable chair and sitting with a straight back?
o: Repetitive strain injury in the fingers
questions.why: Poor posture causes back and neck ache, which an adjustable chair helps prevent; eye strain and glare headaches are reduced by breaks and anti-glare screens.

questions.q: Which is a negative effect of using microprocessor-controlled devices in the home?
o: Heating can be switched on remotely before arriving home
The washing machine can run while the owner is out
People may become lazy and less active as they rely on the devices
Food can be cooked with less supervision
questions.why: Relying on devices to do jobs can lead to a less active, unhealthy lifestyle; the other options are benefits.

long.q: Describe two health problems caused by using a computer for long periods, and one way of reducing each.
scheme: B1: a problem, e.g. repetitive strain injury (RSI) from typing or using a mouse
B1: matching remedy, e.g. ergonomic keyboard or mouse, wrist rest, regular breaks
B1: a second problem, e.g. eye strain and headaches; back or neck pain
B1: matching remedy, e.g. anti-glare screen and breaks; adjustable chair and correct posture

long.q: Many homes now contain microprocessor-controlled devices such as washing machines, smart thermostats and robot vacuum cleaners. Describe two positive and two negative effects of these devices on people's lifestyles.
scheme: B1: a positive effect, e.g. less time spent on housework, so more leisure time
B1: a second positive effect, e.g. devices can be controlled remotely by phone; saves energy by running only when needed
B1: a negative effect, e.g. people become lazy or dependent on the devices and lose household skills
B1: a second negative effect, e.g. less exercise; devices are costly to buy and repair; risk of hacking

long.q: Explain one way smart home devices can improve the security of a home and two ways they can put the owner's data at risk.
scheme: B1: an improvement, e.g. smart cameras and alarms send alerts to the owner's phone; lights can be switched on remotely so the house looks occupied
B1: a risk, e.g. a device connected to the internet can be hacked and used to spy on the household
B1: a second risk, e.g. data about when the owner is out could be stolen and used to plan a burglary; weak default passwords are left unchanged

long.q: Discuss how using smartphones and social media has affected people's social interaction.
scheme: B1: positive: people can keep in touch easily with friends and family who live far away, e.g. video calls and messaging
B1: positive: people can find online communities who share their interests
B1: negative: less face-to-face contact, which can lead to isolation or weaker communication skills
B1: negative: e.g. cyberbullying; pressure to be always available; people ignore those physically with them

long.q: Describe two ways microprocessor-controlled devices in the home can reduce energy use, and one way they can increase it.
scheme: B1: a way of saving energy, e.g. a smart thermostat heats the home only when people are in or about to arrive
B1: a second way, e.g. a washing machine weighs the load and uses only the water and heat needed; lights switch off when a room is empty
B1: an increase, e.g. devices left on standby or always connected use electricity all the time; making and disposing of the devices uses energy

questions.q: An expert system includes a knowledge base and
questions.why: Plus a rules base and user interface.

questions.q: Which is an example of a computer-controlled system?
questions.why: Sensors feed readings to a microprocessor that controls outputs.

questions.q: Which is a use of a computer in a school?
o: Recording attendance with a management system
questions.why: Others: timetables, learning platforms, reports.

questions.q: In an online concert booking system, why is a seat temporarily locked once a customer selects it?
o: To stop the same seat being sold to two customers
To make the website load faster
To encrypt the customer's card details
questions.why: Locking the seat while the booking is completed prevents double booking; the seat is released if the customer does not finish paying.

questions.q: A delivery van's computer works out its exact position from signals sent by several satellites. Which system is this?
questions.why: A GPS receiver calculates its position from the time signals take to arrive from at least three satellites; a GIS displays and analyses data on maps.

long.q: A greenhouse uses a computer-controlled system to keep the temperature between 20 °C and 25 °C. Describe how the system works.
scheme: B1: a temperature sensor measures the temperature
B1: an ADC converts the analogue signal to digital
B1: the microprocessor compares the reading with the preset values (20–25 °C)
B1: below 20 °C it switches the heater on; above 25 °C it opens windows or switches on a fan (using actuators)
B1: the process repeats continuously

long.q: Describe the steps that take place when a customer withdraws cash from an ATM.
scheme: B1: the customer inserts the card and the chip (or magnetic stripe) is read
B1: the customer types in their PIN, which is checked; after three wrong attempts the card is kept
B1: the customer selects the amount to withdraw
B1: the bank's computer checks the account has enough money
B1: the cash is dispensed, the account is debited and a receipt may be printed

long.q: Explain how an online booking system for a concert stops two customers from booking the same seat.
scheme: B1: the seating database is checked in real time, so only available seats are shown
B1: when a customer selects a seat it is locked (held) for a short time so no one else can choose it
B1: once payment is made the record is updated straight away to show the seat as booked

long.q: Describe how a satellite navigation system in a car works out the car's position and gives the driver directions.
scheme: B1: the receiver in the car picks up signals from several (at least three or four) satellites
B1: each signal contains the time it was sent, so the time delay gives the distance to each satellite
B1: the distances are combined (trilateration) to calculate the car's exact position
B1: the position is shown on a stored map and the software calculates a route, giving spoken and on-screen directions

long.q: A town council uses a computer model to decide the timing of traffic lights at a busy junction. Give two advantages and one disadvantage of using a model rather than testing the timings on the real roads.
scheme: B1: an advantage, e.g. no danger to drivers or pedestrians while timings are tried out
B1: a second advantage, e.g. many different timings can be tested quickly and cheaply; no traffic jams are caused
B1: a disadvantage, e.g. the model is only as good as its data and rules, so it may not match real driver behaviour

questions.q: The correct order is
o: analysis, design, development and testing, implementation, documentation, evaluation
questions.why: Analyse first, evaluate last.

questions.q: Parallel running means
o: the old and new systems run together for a time
the new system replaces the old at once
the system is changed in stages
questions.why: Safer but more costly.

questions.q: Test data for a field 'Age' that accepts 11 to 18. Which is extreme data?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates gave explanations instead of test data. Extreme data is on the boundary of what is accepted.

questions.q: Which system implementation strategy runs the new system and old system simultaneously until the new one proves reliable?
questions.why: Parallel running provides a safety net: if the new system fails, the old system continues operation with zero data loss, despite higher running costs.

questions.q: An analyst needs the views of 400 staff in different branches quickly. Which method of researching the current system is most suitable?
questions.why: Questionnaires can be sent to many people at once and answered quickly and anonymously; interviewing or observing 400 people would take far too long.

long.q: Describe two methods of implementing a new system and give one advantage of each.
scheme: B1: direct changeover: the old system is replaced at once
B1: advantage: fast and cheap, benefits immediately
B1: parallel running: both systems run together
B1: advantage: if the new system fails, the old one is still there

long.q: A hospital is switching to a new electronic patient records system. Evaluate direct changeover versus parallel running.
scheme: B1: direct changeover stops the old system overnight and starts the new system immediately: fast and avoids duplicate data entry
B1: high risk with direct changeover: if the new system has critical bugs, patient care could be disrupted with no fallback
B1: parallel running runs both systems side by side until the new one is proven, so there is a fallback if it fails
B1: disadvantage of parallel running: hospital staff must duplicate all entries in both systems, doubling workload and costs

long.q: A systems analyst is researching how a shop's current stock system works. Describe two methods of research the analyst could use and give one disadvantage of each.
scheme: B1: a method, e.g. questionnaires given to staff
B1: matching disadvantage, e.g. staff may not return them or may not answer honestly; no follow-up questions
B1: a second method, e.g. interviews; observation; examining existing documents
B1: matching disadvantage, e.g. interviews are time-consuming; people may work differently when watched; documents may be out of date

long.q: A field Age on a school database must accept whole numbers from 11 to 18. Give one example each of normal, extreme and abnormal test data for this field.
scheme: B1: normal data: a value inside the range, e.g. 14 (should be accepted)
B1: extreme data: a value on the boundary, i.e. 11 or 18 (should be accepted)
B1: abnormal data: a value that should be rejected, e.g. 25, -3 or 'ten'

long.q: Explain the difference between technical documentation and user documentation, giving two items found in each.
scheme: B1: technical documentation helps programmers and analysts maintain, repair or upgrade the system
B1: two items, e.g. program listing/code, file and data structures, system flowcharts, hardware and software requirements
B1: user documentation helps the end user use the system
B1: two items, e.g. how to load or run the software, how to save or print, troubleshooting guide, FAQs, error messages

questions.q: Phishing is
o: fake emails trying to trick you into giving personal details
questions.why: Check sender and links.

questions.q: Encryption
o: makes data unreadable without the key
questions.why: It protects data if intercepted.

questions.q: What is a physical safety risk when using computers?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many thought 'safety' meant damage to the equipment rather than harm to the user.

questions.q: What encryption mechanism uses a public key to encrypt data and a private key to decrypt it?
questions.why: Asymmetric cryptography uses mathematically linked key pairs: anyone can encrypt using the public key, but only the recipient's private key can decrypt.

questions.q: A user types the correct web address but is secretly taken to a fake copy of the website. What is this called?
questions.why: Pharming uses malicious code or a corrupted DNS entry to redirect a correctly typed address to a fake site; phishing relies on the user clicking a link in a fake email.

long.q: Explain two ways a student could protect their personal data online.
scheme: B1: one method, e.g. strong passwords / two-factor authentication
B1: explained: makes unauthorised access harder
B1: a second method, e.g. not opening links in unexpected emails (phishing) / privacy settings
B1: explained

long.q: Explain how two-factor authentication (2FA) significantly improves security when accessing online financial accounts.
scheme: B1: 2FA requires two distinct authentication factors: something you know (password/PIN) and something you have (phone/token) or are (biometric)
B1: if a cybercriminal steals or guesses the password via phishing or data breaches, they cannot gain access without the second factor
B1: the second factor usually generates a time-sensitive, one-time passcode (OTP) that expires rapidly
B1: an unexpected code request warns the genuine owner that someone else has their password

long.q: Describe two physical safety risks in a school computer room and a way of reducing each.
scheme: B1: a risk, e.g. electrocution from damaged cables or drinks spilt near equipment
B1: matching precaution, e.g. check cables regularly; no drinks allowed near computers
B1: a second risk, e.g. tripping over trailing cables; fire from overloaded sockets or overheating equipment
B1: matching precaution, e.g. cable ducts or covers; do not overload sockets, keep vents clear and have a CO₂ extinguisher

long.q: Explain the difference between phishing and pharming.
scheme: B1: phishing: the criminal sends an email that appears to come from a genuine organisation such as a bank
B1: the email contains a link to a fake website where the user is tricked into entering personal details
B1: pharming: malicious code is installed on the user's computer or a DNS server is altered
B1: so the user is redirected to a fake website even when they type the correct web address

long.q: Describe how a user can tell that a website uses a secure (SSL/TLS) connection and explain why this matters when paying online.
scheme: B1: the address begins https:// and a padlock symbol appears in the browser
B1: data sent between the browser and the web server is encrypted
B1: so if card details are intercepted they cannot be read or understood

questions.q: When designing for young children, you should use
o: large text, simple language and images
questions.why: Match the product to its audience.

questions.q: A website is for young children. Which design choice suits the audience?
o: Large text, simple words and bright images
questions.why: Always consider the audience's age and needs.

questions.q: Why find out the audience's needs before designing?
o: So the content, language and design suit them
questions.why: Consider age, experience and accessibility.

questions.q: A presentation is for busy company directors. Which design best suits this audience?
o: Short bullet points with key figures and clear charts
Cartoon images and very simple vocabulary
questions.why: Directors have little time and need the key facts quickly, so concise points and charts suit them; cartoons and heavy animation look unprofessional.

questions.q: Which method helps protect software from being illegally copied and installed?
o: Running a spell check on the program
Saving the files in PDF format
Requiring a unique product key to activate it
questions.why: The software will not install or run without a valid product key or activation code, so an illegal copy is useless; the other options do not restrict use.

long.q: A website is being designed to teach six-year-olds about animals. Describe three ways the design should suit this audience.
scheme: B1: simple language and short sentences
B1: large, clear font with bright colours and plenty of images
B1: simple navigation, e.g. large buttons or icons; sound or animation to keep interest

long.q: Explain why a designer should find out about their audience before creating a presentation, and describe two ways of finding out about the audience.
scheme: B1: so the content, language level and style suit the audience's needs, age and knowledge
B1: so the audience stays interested and understands the message
B1: a method, e.g. a questionnaire or survey of the audience
B1: a second method, e.g. interviews; asking the organiser; looking at what similar audiences have used

long.q: Explain what is meant by software piracy and describe two methods used by software companies to prevent it.
scheme: B1: software piracy is copying, distributing or using software without a valid licence (illegally)
B1: a method, e.g. a product key or activation code that must be entered when installing
B1: a second method, e.g. online activation linked to one device; a dongle; digital rights management; a hologram on the packaging
B1: explanation that the software will not run (fully) without the valid key, licence or device

long.q: A manufacturer is writing a guide to a new machine for expert engineers and another for members of the public. Explain how the two guides should differ.
scheme: B1: the engineers' guide can use technical terms and jargon; the public guide needs plain, simple language
B1: the engineers' guide can include detailed specifications, data and technical diagrams
B1: the public guide needs step-by-step instructions with simple labelled pictures
B1: the public guide needs a clear layout and safety warnings explained fully, as readers have little prior knowledge

long.q: A student wants to use photographs found on the internet in a project that will be published on the school website. Describe what the student should do to avoid breaking copyright law.
scheme: B1: check whether the image is protected by copyright and what its licence allows
B1: ask the copyright owner for permission, or use images that are copyright-free or under a licence such as Creative Commons
B1: acknowledge the source/creator of each image used

questions.q: CC in an email means
o: a copy is sent to another recipient visibly
questions.why: BCC hides recipients.

questions.q: What is the generic name for meeting online with sound and video in real time?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates knew trade names for these meetings but not the generic term.

questions.q: Which is a feature of email that saves time when writing to the same group again?
questions.why: Bcc hides the other recipients' addresses.

questions.q: A teacher emails 30 parents and must not let any parent see the others' email addresses. Where should the parents' addresses be entered?
questions.why: Addresses in BCC receive the email but are hidden from all other recipients; addresses in To and CC are visible to everyone.

questions.q: Which is good netiquette when writing an email?
o: Writing the whole message in capital letters so it stands out
Forwarding chain emails to all your contacts
Including other people's personal details without asking
Avoiding capital letters for whole sentences, as they look like shouting
questions.why: Text in capitals is read as shouting, so it is avoided; forwarding chain emails and sharing other people's details are poor netiquette.

long.q: Explain the difference between CC and BCC when sending an email, and describe a situation where BCC should be used.
scheme: B1: CC sends a copy, and every recipient can see who else received it
B1: BCC sends a copy, but the BCC addresses are hidden from other recipients
B1: e.g. sending a newsletter to many customers so their email addresses stay private

long.q: Explain the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web.
scheme: B1: the internet is the worldwide network of interconnected computer networks (the hardware and connections)
B1: the World Wide Web is the collection of web pages and websites accessed through the internet

long.q: For the web address https://www.cityzoo.org/visit/tickets.html, identify (a) the protocol, (b) the domain name, (c) the file name.
scheme: B1: (a) https
B1: (b) www.cityzoo.org (accept cityzoo.org)
B1: (c) tickets.html

long.q: A student finds information for a history project on a website. Describe four ways the student can judge whether the information is reliable.
scheme: B1: check who wrote it: an expert or a known organisation (e.g. .gov or .ac domain, university, museum)
B1: check when it was last updated, so the information is not out of date
B1: compare the information with other websites, books or sources to see if it agrees
B1: e.g. check for bias or advertising; check for spelling errors; check the site has references or contact details

long.q: Compare a blog and a wiki.
scheme: B1: a blog is a personal website or online journal, usually written by one author
B1: blog posts appear in reverse date order and readers can only comment, not edit the posts
B1: a wiki is a website that many users can create and edit, e.g. an online encyclopedia
B1: wiki pages can be changed by anyone with access, and the edit history is kept so changes can be undone

questions.q: Which file type is best for a photograph on a web page?
questions.why: JPEG compresses photos well.

questions.q: A CSV file stores
o: data as plain text separated by commas
questions.why: Easy to import into spreadsheets and databases.

questions.q: Which file type is best for a photo on a web page?
questions.why: JPEG uses lossy compression to keep photos small.

questions.q: A document must look exactly the same on any computer and should not be easy to edit. Which file type is best?
questions.why: A PDF keeps the layout, fonts and images fixed on any device and is hard to edit; .rtf and .txt are editable text formats.

questions.q: Which statement about lossy compression is correct?
o: Some data is permanently removed to reduce the file size
The original file can be restored exactly
It always makes the file larger
It is used only for text files
questions.why: Lossy compression (as in JPEG and MP3) deletes detail the user is unlikely to notice, so the original cannot be recovered; lossless compression keeps all the data.

long.q: Explain why a large photograph should be compressed before it is placed on a web page, and name a suitable file type.
scheme: B1: a smaller file size means the page loads faster
B1: it uses less bandwidth and storage
B1: a suitable type, e.g. .jpg

long.q: You have written a report that must be opened by a colleague who uses different word-processing software. Describe how you would save the report so they can open it, and name two suitable generic file formats.
scheme: B1: use Save As (or Export) and choose a generic file type from the list, giving a suitable file name
B1: a format, e.g. .rtf (rich text format)
B1: a second format, e.g. .txt (plain text) or .pdf

long.q: Data from a spreadsheet is to be imported into a database. Explain what a .csv file is and why it is a suitable format for this.
scheme: B1: csv stands for comma-separated values
B1: each record is on a new line and the fields are separated by commas
B1: it is a generic text format, so almost any spreadsheet or database software can open or import it

long.q: State what type of file each of these extensions is: (a) .mp3 (b) .png (c) .css (d) .zip
scheme: B1: (a) compressed audio (sound) file
B1: (b) image file (lossless compressed, can have a transparent background)
B1: (c) cascading stylesheet for a web page
B1: (d) compressed (zipped) archive of one or more files

long.q: Explain the difference between lossy and lossless compression, and state which type should be used for a text document and which for a photograph on a web page.
scheme: B1: lossy compression permanently removes some data, so the original cannot be rebuilt exactly
B1: lossless compression reduces the file size without losing any data, so the original is restored exactly
B1: text document: lossless, because losing data would change or corrupt the text
B1: photograph on a web page: lossy (e.g. .jpg), because the file is much smaller and the small loss in quality is hardly noticed

questions.q: To resize an image without distorting it, you should
questions.why: Maintain the proportions.

questions.q: An image is resized without distortion. What has been kept?
questions.why: Lock the aspect ratio before resizing.

questions.q: What does cropping an image do?
o: Removes unwanted outer parts of it
questions.why: Resizing changes its dimensions.

questions.q: An image 800 × 600 pixels is resized with its aspect ratio locked so that its width becomes 400 pixels. What is its new height?
questions.why: Keeping the aspect ratio scales both dimensions by the same factor; the width is halved, so the height becomes 600 ÷ 2 = 300.

questions.q: An image of a car facing left must face right, like a mirror image, without turning upside down. Which tool should be used?
questions.why: Flipping horizontally mirrors the image left to right; rotating by 180° would also turn the car upside down.

long.q: Describe how to make an image half its width in a document without distorting it, and explain how cropping is different from resizing.
scheme: B1: keep (lock) the aspect ratio
B1: e.g. set the width to 50% or drag a corner handle, so the height changes in proportion
B1: cropping removes part of the image; resizing keeps the whole image but changes its size

long.q: An image in a document is facing the wrong way. Describe how to rotate it 90° clockwise and how to flip it horizontally, and explain how flipping differs from rotating.
scheme: B1: select the image, then use the rotate option (Rotate Right 90°) or set the rotation to 90°
B1: use the flip (reflect) horizontal option
B1: rotating turns the whole image around a point; flipping creates a mirror image, swapping left and right

long.q: Explain how reducing the resolution of an image affects its file size and quality, and give one situation where you would do this.
scheme: B1: fewer pixels are stored, so the file size is smaller
B1: the image has less detail and may look blocky (pixelated) if enlarged
B1: e.g. for an image on a web page, so the page loads faster

long.q: An image is placed in a two-column newsletter. Describe three different text-wrapping options and when each would be used.
scheme: B1: square: text flows around a rectangular box surrounding the image, e.g. a photo in a column of text
B1: tight: text follows the outline of the image's shape, e.g. a logo or cut-out picture
B1: top and bottom: text appears only above and below, not beside, e.g. a wide image across the column; (accept in line with text, behind or in front of text, with a suitable use)

long.q: Explain what is meant by the colour depth of an image and the effect of reducing the colour depth.
scheme: B1: colour depth is the number of bits used to store the colour of each pixel
B1: reducing it means fewer colours can be shown, so quality falls, e.g. colour banding
B1: but the file size is smaller

questions.q: A header in a document
o: appears at the top of every page
questions.why: Footers appear at the bottom.

questions.q: What is a widow in document layout?
o: The last line of a paragraph left alone at the top of a page
questions.why: An orphan is the first line left at the bottom of a page.

questions.q: What are margins in a document?
o: The blank space between the text and the edge of the page
questions.why: Gutter margins allow for binding.

questions.q: Which alignment makes both the left and right edges of a paragraph straight?
questions.why: Fully justified text adds space between words so that each line runs from the left margin to the right margin.

questions.q: A newsletter needs text that flows down one column and then continues at the top of the next, side by side on the page. Which feature should be used?
questions.why: Newspaper-style columns let text flow from the bottom of one column to the top of the next; tab stops only line up text along a single line.

long.q: Explain the difference between a widow and an orphan in a document, and how either can be removed.
scheme: B1: widow: the last line of a paragraph on its own at the top of a new page or column
B1: orphan: the first line of a paragraph on its own at the bottom of a page or column
B1: remove with a page or column break, or by turning on widow/orphan control

long.q: Describe how to place an automatic page number and the file name in the footer of a document, and explain why automated fields are better than typing the information.
scheme: B1: open the footer and insert the page number field (e.g. on the right)
B1: insert the file name field (e.g. on the left), so it appears on every page
B1: automated fields update themselves if pages are added or the file is renamed, so they stay correct

long.q: Describe how to insert a table with 4 columns and 6 rows, make the top row a single cell for a title, and add a seventh row at the end.
scheme: B1: insert a table, setting 4 columns and 6 rows
B1: select all the cells in the top row and use merge cells
B1: place the cursor in the last row and insert a row below (or press Tab in the last cell)

long.q: Explain the difference between a page break, a column break and a section break.
scheme: B1: a page break makes the text after it start at the top of a new page
B1: a column break makes the text after it start at the top of the next column
B1: a section break divides the document so each section can have its own layout, e.g. columns, margins or orientation

long.q: A report is in portrait orientation but page 3 holds a wide table. Describe how to make only page 3 landscape.
scheme: B1: insert a section break (next page) before the table
B1: insert another section break (next page) after the table
B1: change the orientation to landscape for that section only, leaving the rest portrait

questions.q: Using styles in a document helps
questions.why: Change a style once and it updates everywhere.

questions.q: Why use a corporate house style?
o: Documents look consistent and the organisation is recognised
questions.why: It sets fonts, colours, logos and layout.

questions.q: Why use styles in a long document?
o: To apply consistent formatting quickly and build a contents page
questions.why: Change a style once and every heading updates.

questions.q: A house style says body text must use a serif font. Which font meets this rule?
questions.why: Times New Roman has small strokes (serifs) at the ends of its letters; Arial, Verdana and Calibri are sans-serif fonts.

questions.q: The Heading 1 style in a long report is changed to Arial 16 point bold. What happens to the headings that already use Heading 1?
o: All of them update automatically to the new format
Only headings typed after the change are updated
Each heading must be reformatted by hand
Only the first heading on each page changes
questions.why: Text that uses a style takes its formatting from that style, so changing the style updates every heading using it at once.

long.q: A company wants all its documents to follow a corporate house style. Explain two benefits of this and give two things the house style would specify.
scheme: B1: consistency: every document looks the same, so the company is recognisable
B1: saves time: staff don't have to choose formatting each time
B1: an item, e.g. font type and size for headings and body text
B1: a second item, e.g. logo position, colour scheme, margins, line spacing

long.q: Explain the difference between a serif font and a sans-serif font, and give an example of each.
scheme: B1: a serif font has small strokes (tails) at the ends of the letters; a sans-serif font has none
B1: a serif example, e.g. Times New Roman, Georgia
B1: a sans-serif example, e.g. Arial, Calibri, Helvetica

long.q: Describe how to create and apply a new paragraph style called Subhead that is Arial, 14 point, bold, centred, with 6 points of space after.
scheme: B1: create a new style and name it Subhead
B1: set the font to Arial, size 14 and bold
B1: set the alignment to centre and the spacing after to 6 pt
B1: select each subheading and apply the Subhead style

long.q: Explain the difference between left-aligned and fully justified text and give a suitable use for each.
scheme: B1: left-aligned text lines up on the left margin with a ragged right edge
B1: fully justified text lines up on both margins; spaces between words are stretched
B1: uses, e.g. left-aligned for letters and web text that must be easy to read; justified for newspaper columns or formal reports

long.q: Explain why it is better to format all the headings in a long report with a heading style than to format each heading by hand.
scheme: B1: every heading looks the same, so the document is consistent
B1: changing the style once updates every heading, saving time
B1: heading styles let the software build an automatic table of contents or navigation pane

questions.q: Validation checks that data is
questions.why: Verification checks it was entered accurately.

questions.q: A range check would stop
o: a typo in a postcode that is still valid
questions.why: It checks a value lies between limits.

questions.q: Which validation check makes sure a date of birth is not in the future?
questions.why: Verification (proof-reading, double entry) checks the data was copied correctly.

questions.q: The sentence 'Meat me at the station' passes a spell check without any error being shown. Why?
o: The spell checker is switched off
'Meat' is a correctly spelt word, even though it is the wrong word here
Spell checkers only check proper nouns
The sentence is too short to be checked
questions.why: A spell checker only checks that each word is in its dictionary, so a real word used in the wrong place is missed; this is why proofreading is still needed.

questions.q: Data is typed in twice by different people and the computer compares the two versions. What is this?
questions.why: Double data entry is a verification method: any difference between the two entries shows a copying error. Range and format checks are validation.

long.q: Explain the difference between validation and verification, with an example of each.
scheme: B1: validation: the computer checks data is reasonable / follows rules
B1: e.g. a range check on age
B1: verification: checks data has been entered or copied accurately
B1: e.g. double entry of a password / visual check

long.q: Explain why a spell checker may not find all the errors in a document.
scheme: B1: a correctly spelt word used in the wrong place is not flagged, e.g. 'there' instead of 'their'
B1: names, specialist terms or other languages may not be in its dictionary, so correct words are flagged or wrong ones accepted
B1: it may be set to the wrong language (e.g. US instead of UK English), and it does not check meaning or layout

long.q: Name the most suitable validation check for each field: (a) Age must be between 11 and 18; (b) Surname must not be left blank; (c) ProductCode must be exactly 6 characters; (d) DateOfBirth must be entered as DD/MM/YYYY.
scheme: B1: (a) range check
B1: (b) presence check
B1: (c) length check
B1: (d) format check

long.q: Explain how a check digit detects an error when a product code is typed in.
scheme: B1: an extra digit is calculated from the other digits and added to the end of the code when it is created
B1: when the code is entered, the computer recalculates the check digit from the digits typed
B1: if the result does not match the check digit entered, an error is shown, e.g. two digits swapped or mistyped

long.q: Apart from spelling, describe four things you should check when proofreading a document before it is printed.
scheme: B1: consistent fonts, sizes and styles for headings and body text
B1: consistent line spacing and spacing between paragraphs
B1: no widows or orphans, and tables or lists not split across pages
B1: e.g. no blank pages; correct page orientation and margins; images in the right place

questions.q: Which chart best shows parts of a whole?
questions.why: Each sector is a share of the total.

questions.q: What should every chart include?
o: A title and labelled axes or a legend
questions.why: Choose the chart type that fits the data.

questions.q: Which chart shows change over time?
questions.why: Pie charts show parts of a whole.

questions.q: A scientist wants to see whether there is a relationship between hours of revision and exam score for 50 students. Which chart is best?
questions.why: A scatter graph plots one variable against the other for each student, so any correlation shows up as a pattern in the points.

questions.q: A chart must show monthly rainfall in mm and average temperature in °C for the same months. What is the best way to show both clearly?
o: Plot one data series on a secondary vertical axis
Use a pie chart for both
questions.why: The two series have different units and ranges, so a secondary axis gives each its own correctly labelled scale.

long.q: A teacher wants to compare the average test scores of four classes. Which type of chart should be used, and what labels must it have? Describe a situation where a pie chart would be better.
scheme: B1: a bar (column) chart, to compare values across categories
B1: a chart title
B1: axis titles and category labels, e.g. 'Class' and 'Average score (%)'
B1: a pie chart shows parts of a whole, e.g. the proportion of students at each grade

long.q: A spreadsheet holds the average temperature for each of the 12 months of a year. State the most suitable type of chart, explain why, and describe how to set the value axis to run from 0 to 35 °C.
scheme: B1: a line graph
B1: because it shows the trend in a value changing over time
B1: format the value (vertical) axis, setting the minimum to 0 and the maximum to 35 (instead of automatic)

long.q: Item names are in A2:A6 and sales figures are in C2:C6. Describe how to create a pie chart of these data showing a percentage on each segment and no legend.
scheme: B1: select A2:A6, then hold Ctrl and select C2:C6 (non-adjacent ranges)
B1: insert a pie chart
B1: add data labels and set them to show the category name and percentage
B1: delete the legend (set legend to none)

long.q: Explain what a secondary value axis is and when a chart needs one.
scheme: B1: a second value axis, usually on the right-hand side of the chart
B1: needed when two data series have very different ranges or units, e.g. rainfall in mm and temperature in °C
B1: one series is plotted against each axis (often as a combined bar and line chart) so both can be read clearly

long.q: A bar chart showing one series has a legend reading 'Series1' and no axis titles. Describe how to improve the chart and explain why its legend can be removed.
scheme: B1: add a meaningful chart title
B1: add titles to both axes, e.g. 'Month' and 'Sales ($)'
B1: with only one data series the legend gives no extra information, so it can be deleted

questions.q: Mail merge combines
o: a master document with a data source
questions.why: To personalise letters for many people.

questions.q: What does a page break do?
o: Starts the following text on a new page
questions.why: A section break can also change layout from that point.

questions.q: What is a header?
o: Text that appears at the top of every page
questions.why: Footers appear at the bottom; both often hold page numbers.

questions.why: Page orientation can only change between sections, so section breaks are needed; a page break starts a new page but keeps the same orientation.

questions.q: In a mail merge letter, what happens to the merge field «FirstName» when the merge is run?
o: It is replaced by each customer's first name from the data source
The word FirstName is printed on every letter
It sorts the data source by first name
It checks the spelling of each name
questions.why: A merge field is a placeholder: for each record, it is filled with that record's value from the data source, making a personalised copy.

long.q: Describe the steps needed to carry out a mail merge to send a personalised letter to 200 customers.
scheme: B1: create the master (standard) letter
B1: link it to the data source, e.g. a spreadsheet or database of customers
B1: insert merge fields (e.g. first name, address) in the right places
B1: preview, then merge to a new document, the printer or email

long.q: A booklet is to be printed on A4 paper with all margins 2 cm and a gutter of 1 cm. Describe how to set this up and explain what the gutter is for.
scheme: B1: in page setup, set the paper size to A4
B1: set the top, bottom, left and right margins to 2 cm
B1: set the gutter to 1 cm (on the left or inside edge)
B1: the gutter adds extra space on the binding edge so text isn't lost when the pages are bound

long.q: A page has a heading across the full width followed by text. Describe how to set out only the text in two columns of equal width with 1 cm between them.

B1: set the columns for that section to two

long.q: A table runs over three pages. Describe how to make its first row appear at the top of each page and shade that row light grey.
scheme: B1: select the first row of the table
B1: turn on 'repeat as header row at the top of each page' in the table properties
B1: apply light grey shading to the selected row

long.q: Explain what a hanging indent is, describe how to set one, and give a situation where it is used.
scheme: B1: the first line of the paragraph starts further to the left than the lines below it
B1: set it in the paragraph settings (special: hanging, with a measurement) or by dragging the ruler markers
B1: e.g. a list of references or a bibliography; numbered or bulleted items

questions.why: No two records share it.

questions.why: Leading zeros would be lost in a number field, and no arithmetic is done on it.

questions.why: A range check verifies that a numeric or date value falls between specified upper and lower allowable boundary values.

questions.why: Both conditions must be true, so AND is needed, and 'after' and 'less than' are strict, so > and < are used rather than >= and <=.

long.q: A library database stores details of its books. Design a table with four fields, give a suitable data type for each, and identify the primary key.

B1: e.g. OnLoan: Boolean (Yes/No)

B1: telephone numbers may contain spaces, brackets or a + sign, which a number field cannot store
B1: no calculations are ever done on telephone numbers

questions.q: A master slide is used to
o: set consistent design across all slides
questions.why: Change it once for every slide.

questions.q: What is a transition in a presentation?

questions.why: An animation moves an object on a slide.

questions.q: What is a master slide used for?
o: Setting the same layout and style on every slide

Advancing slides on each mouse click

Notes the presenter can see that are not shown to the audience on the slides

B1: few words per slide, e.g. short bullet points; a clear sans-serif font

questions.why: SUM with a range.

questions.q: $A$1 in a formula is
questions.why: It doesn't change when copied.

questions.why: >= means greater than or equal to.

questions.why: The relative reference B2 becomes B3 when copied down one row, while the absolute reference $E$1 stays the same.

B1: (d) =IF(B2>=50,"Pass","Fail")

scheme: B1: A5 is relative, so it changes to A6, A7 … when copied down
B1: $B$1 is absolute, so every row still refers to the tax rate cell

B1: the grade table is an absolute range so it stays fixed when copied

B1: TRUE (approximate match) finds the largest boundary that is less than or equal to the mark, e.g. 62 gives B

long.q: Web pages are developed in three layers. Name each layer and state what it is used for.
scheme: B1: content layer: the HTML that holds the structure and content (text, images, links)
B1: presentation layer: the CSS that controls how the content looks (fonts, colours, layout)
B1: behaviour layer: scripts such as JavaScript that make the page interactive

long.q: Explain the difference between an external stylesheet, an internal (embedded) style and an inline style, and state which takes priority if they set different colours for the same element.
scheme: B1: external stylesheet: a separate .css file attached with a link in the head, so it can style many pages
B1: internal style: CSS written in a <style> element in the head section of one page
B1: inline style: a style attribute inside one HTML tag, affecting only that element
B1: the inline style wins, then the internal style, then the external stylesheet (attached before it)
